aging manufacturing processes. The basic working principles and state-of-the-art research
progress of each cooling technology are elaborated in detail. The common engineering bot-
tlenecks, including ultra-high heat flux endurance, packaging process compatibility, fluid
leakage risks and multi-layer interfacial thermal resistance, are summarized, and the future
development trends of this field are clarified. This review can provide comprehensive
theoretical guidance for structural design and large-scale engineering implementation of
near-junction thermal management solutions for various high-power integrated processors,
especially high-computing-power AI accelerators.

Among them, high-power AI accelerators for large-model training act as typical represen-
tatives of HPIPs: the thermal design power (TDP) of a single mainstream training chip
exceeds 700 W [1], and the local heat flux density in high-density computing regions can

devices such as silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) operate under high-voltage
and high-heat-flux conditions, which jointly impose stringent requirements on existing
cooling systems. The sharp rise in device power consumption mainly originates from
the dense integration of tensor computing units driven by expanding parameters of large
AI models, elevated power density of power electronic devices, and interlayer thermal
coupling effects induced by through-silicon via (TSV) in 3D stacking and multi-chiplet het-
erogeneous packaging. The alternating operation of high bandwidth memory (HBM) and
tensor cores further intensifies transient local hotspots, leading to highly spatiotemporally
uneven heat generation across the entire chip under diverse operating conditions.

Excessive power consumption directly increases the core junction temperature of de-
vice active regions. High-temperature conditions aggravate transistor leakage current loss,
shorten device service life and degrade long-term operational reliability. In addition, the
built-in dynamic frequency scaling protection mechanism will be triggered, which directly
limits the rated performance output of HPIPs. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity of
traditional silicon substrates is merely around 150 W/(m·K), and the coefficient of thermal
expansion (CTE) of silicon fails to match thin-film electrodes and interposer materials.
A standalone silicon substrate cannot rapidly dissipate concentrated hotspot heat under
integrated architectures; the absence of high-performance thermal interface material (TIM)
will further enlarge interfacial thermal resistance, forming a universal technical bottle-
neck restricting continuous improvement of overall power density. Therefore, developing
advanced chip-level thermal management technologies, breaking the inherent thermal
conductivity limitations of silicon-based materials, and constructing efficient global heat
conduction and exchange channels serve as the core foundation to guarantee long-term sta-
ble operation of all types of HPIPs and support performance iteration of both AI computing
chips and wide-bandgap power devices. Such technologies are also critical for reducing
the power usage effectiveness (PUE) and improving the comprehensive energy efficiency
of data center systems.

1.2. Strategic Importance of Thermal Management for High-Power Integrated Processors
With the rapid development of high-end integrated circuits, thermal management
for high-power integrated processors (HPIPs) has evolved from a conventional auxiliary
technique into a core technology that determines chip performance, operational reliability,
and industrial competitiveness. According to the U.S. Air Force Avionics Integrity Program
(AVIP), temperature-related stress accounts for approximately 55% of electronic equipment
failures. Therefore, thermal control remains a critical reliability requirement for HPIPs op-
erating under high-power-density and highly integrated conditions [3]. High temperature
accelerates electromigration, negative bias temperature instability, hot carrier injection, and
other degradation mechanisms, causing transistor aging, parameter drift, and permanent
performance deterioration.
As the most thermally stringent subset of HPIPs, high-power AI accelerators face
severe thermal challenges. The thermal design power (TDP) of state-of-the-art AI accel-
erators has reached the kilowatt level. For instance, the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture
achieves a chip GPU exceeding 1000 W [4], and the overall module thermal load approaches
1200 W when integrated with high bandwidth memory (HBM) and dense interconnection
components [5]. The drastically increased on-chip thermal stress and temperature gradi-

limitations, improving energy efficiency and service life, and supporting the continuous
iteration of high-power integrated processors.

1.3. Review Scope and Structure
This review targets advanced chip-level thermal management technologies for HPIPs.
High-power AI accelerators are taken as the core research representative within the HPIP
category, while wide-bandgap power electronic devices are also discussed as supple-
mentary research objects. The overall research scope falls into three major branches:
near-junction liquid cooling, packaging thermal management, and thermal performance
optimization of functional materials. Detailed contents cover core technologies including
microchannel liquid cooling, jet impingement cooling, thermal interface materials (TIMs),
heat pipes and vapor chambers, high-conductivity substrate integration, as well as collab-
orative thermal design tailored for chiplet and three-dimensional integrated circuit (3D
IC) architectures.
The literature search was conducted using the core keywords “High-power AI pro-
cessors”, “Chip-level thermal management”, “Microchannel cooling”, “Thermal interface
materials”, and “High thermal conductivity substrates”. The databases searched include
Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and CNKI (China National Knowledge In-
frastructure). The selected literature covers SCI/EI journal articles, high-level conference
papers, and key Chinese core journals from the past two decades, ensuring both technolog-
ical currency and authority.

1.4. Literature Review Methodology
To comprehensively sort out advanced chip-level thermal management technologies
for high-power heterogeneous integrated chips, this review systematically retrieves the
relevant literature from mainstream databases including Web of Science, IEEE Xplore,
ScienceDirect and CNKI. The retrieval time range covers publications issued from 1981 to
2026. The core search keywords are defined as follows: high-power chip, heterogeneous
integration, chiplet, near-junction cooling, thermal interface material, immersion cooling,
microchannel heat sink, thermal characterization, wide-bandgap device, AI processor.
Clear inclusion and exclusion criteria were formulated for literature screening. The
inclusion criteria are as follows: (1) peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers
focusing on chip-level thermal management, packaging heat dissipation and thermal mea-
surement technology; (2) studies with quantitative experimental data, numerical simulation
results or comparative performance analysis of cooling schemes; (3) research targeting
high-power heterogeneous chips, AI accelerators and wide-bandgap power integrated
devices. The exclusion criteria include the following: (1) patents, book chapters, review
papers without original comparison data; (2) studies only focusing on system-level data
center energy optimization without chip-scale heat dissipation analysis; (3) articles with

2. Heat Generation Characteristics and Thermal Challenges of
High-Power Integrated Processors
2.1. Dual Rise in Power Consumption and Heat Flux Density
For a long time, the semiconductor industry has relied on the synergy of Moore’s
Law and Dennard Scaling to maintain relatively stable power density while increasing
transistor integration. However, as feature sizes approach physical limits, Dennard Scaling
has effectively broken down since the 22 nm node, resulting in power density no longer
decreasing with process scaling [10]. This fundamental shift has transformed the heat
generation issue of high-performance computing chips from a “tolerable byproduct” into
the primary bottleneck restricting performance scaling.
The exponential growth in computing demand in the era of artificial intelligence
has further exacerbated this contradiction. The power consumption of mainstream AI
accelerators has increased significantly, from approximately 400 W for the NVIDIA A100 to
700 W for the NVIDIA H100, while the AMD MI300X reaches a power envelope of about
750 W [11]. However, single-chip TDP is only one aspect of the problem. The real challenge
lies in the fact that this high power is confined to an increasingly small chip area, leading to
a sharp rise in heat flux density. For example, the local hotspot heat flux density of modern

challenge

a sharp rise in heat flux density. For example, the local hotspot heat flux density of modern
AI chips can now exceed 1 kW/cm2, far exceeding the ultimate load-bearing capacity of
traditional air cooling [2].
To complicate matters further, to break through the performance bottleneck of mono-
lithic chips, the industry has shifted from monolithic system-on-chips (SoCs) to 2.5D/3D

nificant thermal interaction paths are formed between adjacent chiplets through-silicon
interposers, micro-bumps, and redistribution layers (RDLs). When an active chip oper-

Early research optimistically believed that using high-thermal-conductivity thermal
interface materials or enhanced convective heat transfer could effectively isolate thermal
effects between chips. However, scholars Virmani and Chatterjee noted [3] that this single-
point optimization approach ignores the non-linear characteristics of multi-scale thermal
coupling. Their analysis shows that in 3D stacked structures, multiple bonding interfaces,
through-silicon vias (TSVs), and underfill layers form complex anisotropic heat conduc-
tion paths, making it often insufficient to suppress overall thermal interaction by simply
reducing the thermal resistance of a single part. On the contrary, excessively increasing the
thermal conductivity of the interposer may instead exacerbate thermal coupling between
hotspots, leading to more uneven temperature distribution. This counterintuitive finding
challenges the traditional design philosophy that “higher material thermal conductivity is
always better”, revealing that thermal management in chiplet systems must be re-examined

traditional thermal management methods increasingly ineffective. Subsequent chapters

this foundation.

2.2. Thermal Management Complexity Brought by Chiplet and 3D IC Architectures
Chiplet and 3D IC architectures break the performance and area bottlenecks of tra-
ditional monolithic chips through heterogeneous integration and vertical stacking, and
have become the mainstream technical route for high-power AI chips. Nevertheless,
such architectural innovation also brings unprecedented thermal management challenges,
whose complexity is continuously exposed and aggravated with the improvement of
integration density.
As early as 2014, Garrou et al. [13] systematically reviewed 3D integration technologies
and pointed out that through-silicon vias, micro-bumps and multi-layer interfacial materials
in vertically stacked structures form a high-resistance heat transfer network. This greatly
increases the thermal resistance between layers, making it difficult for heat in the core
layers to dissipate to external heat sinks, and, thus, exacerbating internal thermal gradients
and hotspot issues within chips. This finding first revealed the inherent bottlenecks of 3D
integration architectures in heat transfer paths, laying an important theoretical foundation
for the subsequent thermal design of chiplets and high-power AI chips, and also alerting
the industry to thermal risks at the architectural level.

therefore constitute indispensable components of the overall thermal management toolkit
